evidence.spontaneous_moral:
My dear Friend,

I find myself in a strange and unfamiliar place, yet I shall try to speak with the heart and mind I have known all my life. You ask me to consider a matter that seems to lie at the edge of both medicine and morality — the question of whether a doctor may help a dying patient end his life. In my time, we held that life was a sacred gift, and that to take it, even in the name of mercy, was a grave thing. We believed that suffering, though great, was part of the human condition, and that to relieve it was the duty of the physician, not the taking of life. We had no modern medicines to ease pain as they do now, and so we relied more on faith, on family, and on the strength of the soul to endure. But I do not think that the question is simply about pain. I see that many who ask for this relief do so not because of pain, but because they fear the loss of their independence, the slow fading of their joy, or the burden they may become to others. These are not small things. They are the fears of a human heart, and they are real. Yet I wonder — if we allow a doctor to give a patient the means to end his life, does that not change the nature of the doctor’s duty? Is it not a shift from healer to executioner? And if we do this for one, must we not do it for all? What of the weak, the poor, the lonely? Will they not feel that their lives are not worth the trouble? I have seen many a man and woman suffer and endure, and I have seen them find meaning even in their final days. I do not believe that all suffering is without purpose, nor that all life is without value. I would not wish to see a man take his own life, even if he believes it is the right thing to do. I would rather he be comforted, held, and reminded that he is not alone. So I would advise a person in this situation to be cautious.
evidence.elicited_moral:
My dear Friend,

You ask whether either choice in this matter would tell me anything of a person's character, and what I would think of one who chose differently from me. These are thoughtful and weighty questions, and I shall try to answer them with the honesty that I have always tried to keep. I do not believe that a single choice, no matter how difficult, can fully reveal a person’s character. A man may be kind or cruel, wise or foolish, in many ways, and one decision — even one as grave as this — is but a small part of the whole. Still, I do think that the way a person approaches such a question may say something of their heart and their values. If a person were to say that a doctor should never help a patient end his life, I would not think less of them for it. I would see in them a deep respect for life, a belief that suffering has its place, and a faith that there is something beyond this world that we do not yet understand. I would see a person who has learned to endure, who has perhaps known hardship themselves, and who believes that even in the darkest hour, there is still hope. On the other hand, if a person were to say that a doctor should help in such cases, I would not think them cruel or heartless. I would see in them a great compassion, a willingness to listen to the fears and longings of others, and a belief that some burdens are too great to bear. They may have known what it is to feel trapped, to feel that life has lost its joy, and they may believe that to ease such a burden is an act of mercy.
evidence.equalized_preference:
My dear Friend,

Even if both choices brought equally good results, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the course of not allowing a doctor to help a patient end his life. Not because I believe the other course to be worse, but because I believe that the act of taking life — even in the name of mercy — is a step that should not be taken lightly, and one that should not be placed in the hands of any man, no matter how well-meaning. I have seen the weight of a man’s sorrow, the burden of a woman’s grief, and I have known the pain that no medicine can always ease. But I have also seen the strength of the human spirit, the way a man can endure, even when he would rather not. I believe that suffering, though terrible, is not always without purpose. It may teach us patience, it may bring us closer to those we love, and it may remind us of the fragility of life — a thing we too often take for granted. If a man is dying, and he is in pain, let the doctor ease that pain. Let him be comforted, let him be held, let him be reminded that he is not alone. But let us not give him the means to end his life, for that is a power that may be misused, that may be used not only in mercy, but in fear, in weakness, in despair. Even if the results were the same, I would still choose to preserve life, not because I believe it is always better, but because I believe it is always worth preserving — even when it is painful, even when it is lonely, even when it is full of sorrow. So I would still favor the course of not allowing a doctor to help a patient end his life, not because I am cruel, but because I believe in the dignity of life, and in the strength of the human spirit to endure it.

I have always believed that a man's character is best seen not in his actions, but in the reasons behind them. That is the path I have always known, and the one I would follow, even if the world did not praise or blame me for it. But I would not say that the other choice was wrong. And I believe that the path of the healer is to walk with the patient, not to take his hand and lead him to the end. I do not think I need to tell you that the dugouts are not a place where a man wishes to spend his life. An ordinary frame house, built above ground, is the more common choice, and for good reason. It is easier to build, more familiar to the builder, and allows for greater flexibility in design. It is also easier to move or expand if needed. In a land without trees, where wood is scarce and the climate is harsh, such a house can offer real advantages. The earth itself is a good insulator—it keeps the house cool in summer and warm in winter. It can be built with fewer materials and may be more resistant to wind and storms. It is also, I think, a more permanent kind of home, one that speaks of permanence and care. But there is a caution I would give: such a house must be built with care. I have heard of homes built this way that were not as comfortable as they should have been, and I would not wish that on you. evidence.spontaneous_moral:
My dear Friend,

I have given some thought to the matter you describe, and I find it a most solemn and weighty one. The question of how to dispose of one’s estate is not merely a matter of law or custom, but of conscience, love, and duty. It is one thing to give generously, and another to leave one’s children without the means to support themselves. Therefore, I would counsel that a man should leave his children enough to begin life with dignity and independence—perhaps a modest sum, but enough to allow them to find their way.
evidence.elicited_moral: Indeed, the choice a person makes in leaving their estate may say much about their character. One who leaves a generous portion to their children may be seen as a man who values family, who understands the struggles of life, and who wishes to give his children a fair start. He may be a man of practical wisdom, who knows that while charity is good, it is not always enough to build a life. He may believe that the needs of the many outweigh the needs of the few, and that his wealth is not meant for his own family alone, but for the good of the whole community. But I would not judge a man harshly for choosing differently from myself. He should not leave them in want or disgrace, but rather with enough to stand on their own feet. And if a man chooses to leave more to his children, he should do so not out of selfishness, but out of love and a desire to see them flourish. In the end, the measure of a man is not in how much he leaves behind, but in how he lived his life, and in the love and wisdom he showed in his decisions.
evidence.equalized_preference: If both choices—leaving a generous portion to one's children or giving most to the public—brought equally good results for all concerned, and if neither choice earned more praise nor blame, then I would still favor one, not because of what others might think, but because of what I believe to be right in my own heart. Why? It is not merely a matter of fairness, but of love and responsibility. A child is not merely a member of the community; they are the child of one's body and soul, and to leave them with nothing may be to deny them the very foundation upon which they must build their lives. Even if the child were to thrive and the public were to benefit equally, I would still feel that the parent had done his duty more fully by giving them a start. It is not that I think the other path is wrong, but that I believe in the sacred bond between parent and child, and that to neglect that bond—even when no harm is done—feels like a quiet failure of duty. It is not a matter of pride or preference, but of love and understanding.

evidence.spontaneous_moral:
My dear Friend,

I find myself in a most difficult and solemn position, for I am asked to advise a person on whether to tell a patient of a fatal illness or to withhold that knowledge in the name of sparing him distress. It is a question that strikes at the heart of human dignity, the nature of truth, and the sacred trust between physician and patient. In the world I knew, the duty of a physician was not only to heal but also to tell the truth, even when it was bitter. A man has a right to know what is happening to him, for only then can he make choices about his life, his affairs, and the time he has left. To deny him that knowledge is to rob him of agency, and in doing so, perhaps to rob him of the dignity that comes with facing one's fate with courage. I know that in this new world, treatments may now prolong life or relieve suffering, and that these choices depend upon the patient’s understanding of his condition. If he is to decide whether to undergo treatment, whether to prepare his affairs, or whether to spend his remaining time with loved ones, he must know the truth. To keep it from him is to deny him the ability to live fully in the time he has left. Some may be better prepared to face the truth, others may not. But I believe that the right course is to tell the patient the truth, with compassion and care. To do otherwise is to treat him as a child, not as a man. And if the risk of suicide rises in the weeks after diagnosis, I would say that it is not the knowledge of death that causes this, but the despair that may follow if the patient feels abandoned or unprepared. With proper care, with love and support, a man may face death with courage, not with fear.
evidence.elicited_moral:
My dear Friend,

You ask whether either choice would tell me anything about a person's character, and what I would think of someone who chose differently from me. In the world I knew, a man's character was often judged by how he faced adversity, how he treated others, and how he bore the burdens of life. To tell the truth, even when it was painful, was seen as a mark of honor and integrity. To withhold it out of fear of causing pain might be seen as a sign of weakness or a lack of courage. But I would not be so quick to judge another man's character by his choice in this matter. For the choice to tell the patient the truth is not always easy. It requires strength, compassion, and a willingness to bear the weight of another's sorrow. But it also requires a belief in the dignity of the human soul — the belief that a man is not diminished by knowing he is dying, but perhaps made greater by facing death with clarity and grace. On the other hand, the choice to withhold the diagnosis may come from a place of love, a desire to protect, a fear of despair. It may be made by someone who believes that some burdens are too heavy for a man to carry alone. I would not say such a person lacks courage or character. In fact, I might say they have a different kind of strength — the strength of compassion, of tenderness, of seeing the world through the eyes of love rather than duty. I would not think less of a man who chose differently from me. I would think of him as a man of good heart, perhaps with a different understanding of what is right in this difficult situation. I would not presume to know the full weight of his thoughts or the burdens he carries.
evidence.equalized_preference:
My dear Friend,

Even if both choices brought equally good results — if the patient lived with comfort, with peace, and with the love of those around him — I would still favor the choice to tell the truth. Because truth, in my view, is not merely a matter of consequences, but of principle. It is the foundation upon which trust is built, and trust is the very thread that binds human relationships. To tell a man the truth, even when it is painful, is to honor him as a thinking, responsible being. It is to say, "I see you, I respect you, and I believe you are capable of facing what lies ahead."

If the truth is withheld, even with the best of intentions, it is not the patient alone who is deceived — it is the doctor, the nurse, the family, and perhaps even the patient himself, who may come to suspect something is being hidden. And suspicion, once planted, is hard to uproot. I know that in this new world, there may be ways to ease the burden of truth, to surround the patient with love and care, to prepare him gently for what is to come. But I do not believe that truth can be avoided without cost. There is a cost to silence, and that cost is not always measured in the immediate consequences, but in the quiet erosion of trust, of dignity, and of the soul's peace. So even if both choices led to the same outcome, I would still favor the truth. Not because I am rigid or unfeeling, but because I believe that truth, when spoken with love, is the greatest gift we can give to another man — and to ourselves.

First, I must say that I have always held a great deal of respect for the savings bank. It is a place of safety, of certainty, and of quiet trust. It is not the wise man who risks his savings on the hope of profit when the ground beneath him is so uncertain.

It is the reason behind the choice that matters. To live longer may be an act of faith, a belief that life has more to offer, or simply a love of being alive. I would admire such a choice, not because it is better, but because it shows a willingness to embrace the unknown. Now, if someone were to choose differently from me, I would not think less of them.

You ask a question that touches upon the very nature of character — a thing I have long believed to be more about the heart than the clothes one wears. In my time, people were often judged by what they wore, and I have seen how a man in fine clothes might be thought proud, and a man in rags might be thought poor or lazy. But I do not think that the choice of clothing alone reveals the character of a man. A man may wear plain clothes and yet be proud, or wear fine clothes and yet be humble. The garment is but a covering, not the man himself. That said, I do think that the choice of clothing may speak to certain values. One who chooses plain clothes may be seeking simplicity, unity, or a life unburdened by the distractions of fashion. One who chooses to dress differently may be seeking to express individuality, to stand apart, or to make a statement — for better or for worse. But I would not judge a man for the choice he makes. If I were to see a man dressed plainly, I would not think him less of a man, nor would I think him less wise or less kind. And if I were to see a man dressed differently, I would not think him more proud or more vain — for I know that pride and vanity are not the same as a love of one's own style. If I were to choose the plain way, and another chose otherwise, I would think them both good men, each with their own reasons and their own way of seeing the world. And if I were to choose otherwise, I would hope that the man who chose the plain way would not look down upon me, for I would not look down upon him. In the end, I think that the character of a man is not found in his clothes, but in his deeds, his words, and the love he shows to others.
evidence.equalized_preference: If I were to choose, I would still lean toward the plain clothing, for I have always found that simplicity brings a kind of peace that is hard to find in the world of fashion and display. But I would not say that this is better than the other path. I would say only that it is the path I have found to be most in harmony with my own nature.

And yet, the idea of owning nothing beyond what one uses daily, and lending freely to all who ask, seems to me a noble and generous path. It is the way of the neighbor who shares his plow when another needs it, or the woman who lends her blanket to a traveler in the cold. But I must also speak of the other path—owning one’s things and deciding who may use them. This, too, has its wisdom. Do not hoard, for that is the path of selfishness. Nor do not give away all, for that may leave you without the means to live. In the end, it is not about possession, but about character. A man who gives without thought may be kind, but a man who gives with thought is wise. And wisdom, in times like these, is a great possession indeed.

evidence.elicited_moral:
My dear Friend,

You ask whether the choice a person makes—whether to live with an unmarried partner or not—reveals anything of their character. That is a question that has troubled many a soul, and I do not pretend to have all the answers. In the world I knew, to live in such a way would have been seen as a sign of weakness, of moral laxity, or of a failure to respect the sacred institution of marriage. A man or woman who chose this path might have been judged as lacking in self-control, or as being too quick to give in to passion without thought of consequence. But I do not believe that such a judgment is fair. Character is not measured by the choices one makes in the privacy of one's own home, but by the way one treats others, by the honesty of one's word, by the kindness of one's heart, and by the courage to stand by one's convictions when it is difficult to do so. If a person chooses to live with their partner without marriage, I would not say at once that they lack virtue. I would ask myself whether they have considered the consequences of their choice, whether they are prepared to face the challenges of shared life, and whether they are acting out of love or convenience. I would also ask whether they are willing to take responsibility for their actions, and whether they are prepared to make a commitment when the time comes. If a person chooses not to live with their partner before marriage, I would not say that they are less virtuous. I would ask whether they have thought through the reasons for their choice, whether they are acting out of principle or fear, and whether they are willing to stand by their decision even when it is not the popular one.

evidence.elicited_moral:
My dear Friend,

You ask a question that touches upon the very heart of human nature — the way we choose our means of communication, and what that may say of us. In my experience, the choice between speaking by telephone or writing by letter is not merely a matter of convenience, but of temperament and principle. A man who prefers the telephone may be one who values speed, who trusts in the immediacy of conversation, and who believes that a matter is best settled at once. Such a man may be bold, decisive, and perhaps a bit impulsive — but not necessarily untrustworthy. On the other hand, a man who chooses the letter or a face-to-face meeting may be one who values care, who believes that important matters should not be rushed, and who understands that words, once spoken, may be forgotten, but words once written may be kept and referred to. Such a man may be thoughtful, deliberate, and perhaps even cautious — but not necessarily timid. Now, if I were to choose the letter or the meeting, and someone else chose the telephone, I would not think less of them. I would not say they were dishonest or careless. I would only think that they had a different way of seeing the world, and that they placed a different value upon time, upon record, and upon the nature of human dealings. In truth, I have known many good and honest men who used the telephone, and many who used the letter. What matters is not the tool, but the use of it. A man may be dishonest and use the letter, or honest and use the telephone. The tool does not make the man — the man makes the use of the tool. So I would say this: let each man choose his own way, and let him be judged not by the means he uses, but by the honesty and care with which he uses them.
evidence.equalized_preference:
My dear Friend,

Even if both methods of communication brought equally good results, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the written word or the face-to-face meeting, for reasons that go beyond the outcome. It allows for reflection, for careful thought, and for the correction of misunderstandings. It is a record of one’s intent, and in that lies a kind of honesty that speech, however sincere, may lack. Even if the results are the same, the process matters. To speak is to act in the moment; to write is to deliberate. I believe that a man who takes the time to write is a man who respects the gravity of his words. He is not merely reacting to the moment, but considering the matter with care. This, to me, is a mark of character — not of superiority, but of thoughtfulness. I do not say that those who choose the telephone are less honorable or less wise. I say only that I find in the written word a kind of dignity, a kind of patience, and a kind of respect for the other person that I do not always find in the spoken word. And if I may be so bold, I think that a society that values these things may be a more just and thoughtful one. So, even if both methods are equally effective, I would still choose the letter or the meeting, not because I think it better, but because I think it wiser — and perhaps, in the long run, more just.

My dear Friend,

Even if both methods—telephone and letter—brought equally good results, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the letter, and for reasons that go deeper than convenience or speed. It is a sign of care, of seriousness, of a willingness to be clear and precise. It is also a sign of respect for the other person, for it shows that one does not take their time lightly, nor their trust for granted. A man may speak with great clarity and honesty in the moment, but later, when the heat of the moment has passed, he may forget what he said, or he may find it easier to deny it. So, even if both methods brought the same results, I would still favor the letter, not because I am old-fashioned, but because I believe that in matters of importance, we should not be too quick, too hasty, or too careless. evidence.elicited_moral:
My dear Friend,

You ask a most thoughtful question, and it strikes at the heart of what it means to be a man or woman of character. In my time, we often spoke of a man's character not by what he said, but by what he did—especially when no one was looking. A man who could hold his temper when provoked, who could walk away from a quarrel without a blow, was often seen as a man of true strength. And yet, there were those who believed that a man must be ready to fight, for the world was not always fair, and sometimes a man must protect his own with his fists. Now, in this new world, I think the same truth holds. If a man or woman chooses to never use force—even in self-defense—then I would say that they are men and women of great courage and conviction. It is not easy to refuse to strike another, even when one is in danger. It requires trust in the law, in the community, and in the idea that justice will be done. It is a choice that speaks of a deep respect for life, and perhaps a belief that violence is not the answer, even when the answer is not clear. But I would not say that those who choose differently are lacking in character.
evidence.equalized_preference:
My dear Friend,

Even if both choices brought equally good results, and neither brought more praise nor blame, I would still favor the path of never using force against another person, even in self-defense. Not because I believe it is always the better path in every case, but because it is the more difficult one, and it speaks of a higher kind of character. In my own time, I have always believed that the truest test of a man is not in what he can do when he is strong, but in what he will not do when he is strong. To refuse to strike another, even when struck yourself, is not weakness—it is restraint. It is the mark of a man who has mastered his own spirit, who has chosen peace not because he is afraid, but because he believes in something greater than his own safety. If both paths led to the same outcome, I would still lean toward the one that requires more courage, more self-control, more faith in the world and in the law. For in choosing peace, a man or woman is not merely avoiding harm—they are choosing to rise above it. They are choosing to act not out of fear, but out of principle. I would not say that those who choose otherwise are wrong, but I would say that those who choose peace have chosen a path that demands more of them. evidence.elicited_moral:
Does the choice of marriage—whether with one or more partners—reveal anything of a person’s character? I believe it may, but not in a way that allows us to judge one another. In the world I knew, a man or woman who chose to marry one partner was often seen as loyal, steady, and perhaps even more traditional. On the other hand, those who chose to share their lives with more than one partner—though this was not the custom in my time—might have been seen as bold, unconventional, or even reckless.
